## 4. Git Repository and Branch Protection

Version control is the base of every later week. This section follows the order in which the work was done. Each step has its screenshot and an explanation of what every command or screen means, so that a reader who did not sit next to you can follow it.

### 4.1 Creating the Remote Repository (Figure 1)

The first step was to create an empty repository on GitHub. Figure 1 shows the "Create a new repository" form just before it was submitted.

![GitHub "Create a new repository" form: owner SeharMehar, name Campus Notes, visibility Public, README off, no .gitignore, no licence.](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 1.** *GitHub "Create a new repository" form: owner SeharMehar, name Campus Notes, visibility Public, README off, no .gitignore, no licence.*

| **Field**       | **Value in the screenshot**                                    | **Why it matters**                                                                                                     |
|-----------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Owner           | SeharMehar                                                     | The account that owns the repository and controls its settings.                                                        |
| Repository name | "Campus Notes"; GitHub shows "will be created as Campus-Notes" | GitHub allows only letters, digits and ., -, \_, so the space becomes a hyphen. The clone URL is .../Campus-Notes.git. |
| Description     | Empty (0 / 350)                                                | Can be added later. A one-line description makes the repository easier to find.                                        |
| Visibility      | Public                                                         | Anyone can read the code. This is acceptable for coursework only if no secret is ever committed (Section 4.4).         |
| Add README      | Off                                                            | The local project already has a README. Creating one on GitHub would make the first push conflict.                     |
| Add .gitignore  | No .gitignore                                                  | The Next.js project already contains its own .gitignore.                                                               |
| Add license     | No license                                                     | A licence can be added later if the project is shared beyond the course.                                               |

### 4.2 Initializing Git and Making the First Commit (Figure 2)

In PowerShell, inside the campus-notes folder, the repository was initialized and connected to GitHub. A working branch named dev was created, everything was staged and the first commit was made.

![PowerShell: git init, git remote add origin, git checkout -b dev, git add ., git commit -m "Week 5 scaffolding and auth setup" (root commit 820b0a3, 27 files, 10,469 insertions).](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 2.** *PowerShell: git init, git remote add origin, git checkout -b dev, git add ., git commit -m "Week 5 scaffolding and auth setup" (root commit 820b0a3, 27 files, 10,469 insertions).*

| **Command (as run)**                                                 | **What it does**                                                         | **Result shown in Figure 2**                                              |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| git init                                                             | Turns the folder into a Git repository by creating a hidden .git folder. | "Initialized empty Git repository in C:/Users/User/campus-notes/.git/"    |
| git remote add origin https://github.com/SeharMehar/Campus-Notes.git | Registers the GitHub repository under the short name origin.             | No output (success is silent).                                            |
| git checkout -b dev                                                  | Creates a new branch dev and switches to it.                             | "Switched to a new branch 'dev'"                                          |
| git add .                                                            | Stages every file in the folder for the next commit.                     | Warnings "LF will be replaced by CRLF" for each text file.                |
| git commit -m "Week 5 scaffolding and auth setup"                    | Records the staged files as one snapshot with a message.                 | "\[dev (root-commit) 820b0a3\] ... 27 files changed, 10469 insertions(+)" |

> **About the CRLF warnings**
>
> Windows ends lines with CRLF and Linux with LF. Git warns that it will convert line endings the next time it touches the files. The warnings are harmless. Adding a .gitattributes file that fixes the setting (Section 4.7) removes them.

The commit listing in Figure 2 shows what the first snapshot contains: .gitignore, AGENTS.md, README.md, the pages app/admin/page.tsx, app/course/\[id\]/page.tsx, app/login/page.tsx and app/quiz/\[id\]/page.tsx, app/layout.tsx, app/page.tsx, app/globals.css, app/favicon.ico, lib/supabase.ts, the configuration files (eslint.config.mjs, next.config.ts, package.json, package-lock.json, tailwind.config.ts, tsconfig.json), the public/ images and the weekly notes starting with week1.md. A root commit has no parent, which is why Git writes "(root-commit)". The abbreviated number 820b0a3 is the commit's identifier and appears again on GitHub in Figure 4.

### 4.3 Renaming the Branch and Pushing (Figure 3)

The code was then published to GitHub under the branch name main.

![PowerShell: git branch -M main, git push -u origin main (38 objects, 765 KiB), then "nothing to commit, working tree clean" and "Everything up-to-date".](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 3.** *PowerShell: git branch -M main, git push -u origin main (38 objects, 765 KiB), then "nothing to commit, working tree clean" and "Everything up-to-date".*

| **Output line**                                                                       | **Meaning**                                                                                      |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Enumerating objects: 38, done. / Counting objects: 100% (38/38)                       | Git found 38 objects (files, folders and the commit) that GitHub does not have yet.              |
| Delta compression using up to 8 threads / Compressing objects: 100% (30/30)           | Git compressed the data using 8 processor threads before sending.                                |
| Writing objects: 100% (38/38), 765.00 KiB \| 4.87 MiB/s                               | The upload: 765 KiB at 4.87 MiB per second.                                                      |
| Total 38 (delta 3), reused 0 ... pack-reused 0 / remote: Resolving deltas: 100% (3/3) | GitHub received everything and rebuilt the 3 delta-compressed objects.                           |
| To https://github.com/SeharMehar/Campus-Notes.git / \* \[new branch\] main -\> main   | The remote did not have a main branch; it was created.                                           |
| branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'                                           | Because of -u, later git push and git pull need no extra arguments.                              |
| nothing to commit, working tree clean (after git commit -m "Initial commit")          | Nothing was left to record; every file was already committed. This is a good sign, not an error. |
| Everything up-to-date                                                                 | The local and remote branches are identical.                                                     |

> **Side effect of git branch -M main**
>
> This command renames the **current** branch, which was dev, to main. The result is a single branch (see Figure 4: "1 Branch"). The dev branch no longer exists and has to be created again (Section 4.6).

> **Secrets check passed**
>
> A public repository is safe only while no secret is committed. The file list proves that .env was left out, because the default Next.js .gitignore ignores .env files. If a key is ever pushed by mistake, treat it as leaked: create a new key in Supabase first, then remove the old one from the code.

### 4.5 Protecting the main Branch (Figure 5)

In the repository's **Settings \> Branches**, a branch protection rule was added for main. GitHub confirmed it with the banner "Branch protection rule created", and the rule list shows main with "Currently applies to 1 branch". GitHub also advertises Repository Rulesets, the newer mechanism; the existing rule can be converted with the "Convert to ruleset" button.

![GitHub Settings \> Branches: banner "Branch protection rule created"; rule "main" applies to 1 branch.](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 5.** *GitHub Settings \> Branches: banner "Branch protection rule created"; rule "main" applies to 1 branch.*

The screenshot proves that a rule exists but not which options are switched on. Open the rule (**Settings \> Branches \> main \> Edit**) and compare it with the recommended settings below, then capture a screenshot of the enabled options.

| **Setting**                                         | **Recommended value**                                                                                   | **Risk it removes**                                           |
|-----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Require a pull request before merging               | ON                                                                                                      | Unreviewed code reaching main; every change leaves a record.  |
| Required approvals                                  | 1 when a teammate or supervisor is added; 0 for a single developer (the pull request is still required) | GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request. |
| Dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed | ON                                                                                                      | An approved pull request being changed afterwards.            |
| Require status checks to pass before merging        | ON, once an automatic build check exists                                                                | Merging code that does not build.                             |
| Require conversation resolution                     | ON                                                                                                      | Review comments being ignored.                                |
| Block force pushes                                  | ON                                                                                                      | History being rewritten and work lost.                        |
| Restrict deletions                                  | ON                                                                                                      | Accidental deletion of main.                                  |
| Include administrators                              | ON when the project is stable; OFF while setting up, so you cannot lock yourself out                    | The owner bypassing the rules by habit.                       |

> **Proof of protection**
>
> The strongest evidence is a refused push. After the rule is active, try git push origin main with a new commit: GitHub should reject it with a message that the branch is protected. Capture that message as the screenshot for this deliverable.

### 4.6 Branching Model

A small project with one developer still benefits from a strict flow. It keeps main deployable and gives every change a review point.

| **Branch**       | **Purpose**                                                          | **Who pushes**                      | **Merges into**      |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|----------------------|
| main             | Production-ready code that the supervisor sees and that is deployed. | Nobody directly; pull request only. | none                 |
| dev              | Integration branch where finished features are tested together.      | Pull request from a feature branch. | main by pull request |
| feature/\<name\> | One feature or task, for example feature/login-page.                 | The developer.                      | dev                  |
| fix/\<name\>     | A bug fix, for example fix/admin-redirect.                           | The developer.                      | dev                  |

> **Action: create dev again**
>
> Figure 4 shows one branch. To restore the model, switch to main, create dev from it and push it once with git push -u origin dev. From then on, start every task from dev.

The working cycle is: update dev, create a feature branch, commit with a clear message, push the branch, open a pull request into dev, merge when the checks pass, and finally open a pull request from dev into main.

Commit message convention

Messages follow the pattern **type(scope): short description** in the present tense. The first commit, "Week 5 scaffolding and auth setup", is clear but covers many things; smaller commits make the history easier to read and to undo.

| **Type** | **Use for**                            | **Example**                                   |
|----------|----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| feat     | A new feature                          | feat(auth): add signup form                   |
| fix      | A bug fix                              | fix(admin): redirect to login when signed out |
| docs     | Documentation only                     | docs: add week 5 report                       |
| chore    | Tooling or configuration               | chore: add gitattributes                      |
| refactor | Restructure without changing behaviour | refactor(lib): move client to lib/supabase.ts |

## 5. Project Scaffolding

Scaffolding means creating the empty but correctly organized project that every later feature plugs into. A good scaffold makes it obvious where each new file belongs, so the team does not have to decide that again for every feature.

### 5.1 How the Project Was Generated

The project is a standard Next.js starter. Several details in the screenshots show this: the browser tab is titled "Create Next App" (Figure 7), the repository contains AGENTS.md, eslint.config.mjs and next.config.ts, and the public/ folder holds the default starter images file.svg, globe.svg, next.svg, vercel.svg and window.svg (Figure 2). The app/ folder sits directly in the project root, which means the project was created without a src folder, and the App Router was chosen (the app/ folder with layout.tsx and page.tsx).

> **What the App Router means**
>
> In the App Router a **folder is a URL segment** and a file named page.tsx is the screen shown at that address. A folder named in square brackets, such as \[id\], is a **dynamic segment**: one file serves every value, for example /course/12 and /course/45. layout.tsx wraps every page with shared parts such as fonts and the page frame.

### 5.2 Directory Structure (Figure 6)

![VS Code explorer of campus-notes: app (admin, course/\[id\], login, quiz/\[id\], favicon.ico, globals.css, layout.tsx, page.tsx), lib/supabase.ts, node_modules, public, .env.](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 6.** *VS Code explorer of campus-notes: app (admin, course/\[id\], login, quiz/\[id\], favicon.ico, globals.css, layout.tsx, page.tsx), lib/supabase.ts, node_modules, public, .env.*

| **Path**                   | **What it is**                      | **Address / role**                                                      |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| app/page.tsx               | Home page                           | /: course directory (Week 4 Wireframe 1)                                |
| app/layout.tsx             | Root layout                         | Wraps every page; loads globals.css                                     |
| app/globals.css            | Global styles                       | Tailwind CSS directives and base styles                                 |
| app/admin/page.tsx         | Administrator page                  | /admin: manage courses, modules, MCQ banks (Figure 7)                   |
| app/course/\[id\]/page.tsx | Course / module reader              | /course/\<id\>: one course by its id                                    |
| app/quiz/\[id\]/page.tsx   | Quiz screen                         | /quiz/\<id\>: one quiz by its id                                        |
| app/login/page.tsx         | Sign-in page                        | /login: authentication screen (open in the editor tab list of Figure 7) |
| app/favicon.ico            | Browser tab icon                    | Static asset                                                            |
| lib/supabase.ts            | Database client                     | The single place where the connection to Supabase is created            |
| public/                    | Static files                        | Served as they are, for example images                                  |
| .env                       | Environment variables               | Project URL and publishable key (Figure 8); not tracked by Git          |
| node_modules/, .next/      | Installed packages and build output | Generated; ignored by Git                                               |

> **Good structural choices**
>
> The database client lives in lib/, not inside a page, so every page can reuse it. Pages are separated by purpose (public reader, quiz, admin, login), which matches the use cases of the SRS. Sensitive values live in .env, outside the tracked code.

### 5.6 Environment Variables (Figure 8)

Settings that differ between machines, or that must not be public, are kept in environment variables instead of in the code. Figure 8 shows the .env file with two lines.

![.env file with NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY (the key value is hidden in this report).](data:image/png;base64,)

**Figure 8.** *.env file with NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY (the key value is hidden in this report).*

| **Variable**                  | **Meaning**                                                                                                                                                      | **Public?**    |
|-------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------|
| NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL      | The web address of the Supabase project (https://\<project\>.supabase.co).                                                                                       | Yes            |
| NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY | The publishable key (it starts with sb_publishable\_). It identifies the application to Supabase. What it may do is limited by Row Level Security (Section 6.6). | Yes, by design |

- **The prefix NEXT_PUBLIC\_ means "send to the browser".** Next.js copies such variables into the downloaded page code, so they must never hold a secret. A publishable key is meant to be public; a secret key is not.

- **Restart after editing.** Next.js reads .env when the development server starts, so changes need npm run dev to be restarted.

- **Do not commit it.** .env is ignored by Git (Figure 4 confirms it is not on GitHub). Keep a .env.example with names but no values for other developers.

- **Never show a secret key.** If a server-side key (named sb_secret\_... in the Supabase dashboard) is added in a later week, it must not carry the NEXT_PUBLIC\_ prefix and must never appear in a screenshot.

### 6.2 Tables Compared with the Week 4 Design

The Week 4 database design defined 12 tables: the 10 entities of the ERD plus two junction tables. Figure 9 shows exactly those 12, so the database matches the design.

| **Table**        | **ERD entity** | **Purpose**                                             | **Main links**                                     |
|------------------|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| users            | User           | Account record: name, e-mail, role (ADMIN or STUDENT)   | Parent of admins and students                      |
| admins           | Admin          | Administrator profile                                   | 1:1 with users; creates courses                    |
| students         | Student        | Student profile                                         | 1:1 with users; owns progress and results          |
| courses          | Course         | A university subject                                    | Has many modules; created by an admin              |
| enrollments      | junction       | Which student opened which course (M:N)                 | students and courses                               |
| modules          | Module         | A note unit of a course                                 | Belongs to a course; has ai_summaries and one quiz |
| ai_summaries     | AI Summary     | Saved summary and 4 takeaways of a module               | modules                                            |
| progress         | Progress       | Completion and last visited module of one student       | 1:1 with students                                  |
| progress_modules | junction       | Completed modules of a student (N:M)                    | progress and modules                               |
| quizzes          | Quiz           | The quiz of one module                                  | 1:1 with modules; has many mcqs                    |
| mcqs             | MCQ            | A question with options, correct option and explanation | Belongs to a quiz                                  |
| quiz_results     | Quiz Result    | One attempt of a student on a quiz                      | students and quizzes                               |

### 6.3 How the Application Connects

The connection has three parts that work together:

1.  **Configuration:** the project address and the publishable key are stored in .env (Figure 8).

2.  **Client:** lib/supabase.ts (Figure 6) reads those two values and creates one database client for the whole application.

3.  **Use:** pages import that client to read courses, modules and quizzes, to save data, and to handle sign-in and sign-out.

Every request travels over HTTPS to the Supabase project address. The publishable key tells Supabase which project and application the request belongs to; the permissions are then decided by Supabase's Row Level Security rules and, for signed-in users, by the user's session token.

| **Key**                                                      | **Where it may be used**      | **What it can do**                                                    | **Public?** |
|--------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------|
| Publishable key (sb_publishable\_..., older name "anon key") | Browser code, lib/supabase.ts | Only what Row Level Security allows for visitors and signed-in users. | Yes         |
| Secret key (sb_secret\_..., older name "service role key")   | Server code only              | Full access; ignores Row Level Security.                              | Never       |

### 6.5 Rules for Keys

- Only the publishable key may appear in browser code.

- A secret key must never be placed in a screenshot, a chat message or a commit.

- If a secret is exposed, create a new key in Supabase (**Settings \> API Keys**), update .env and any hosting settings, then delete the old key. Do this before anything else.

### 6.6 Row Level Security (RLS)

Row Level Security is a database feature that decides, row by row, who may read or write a table. When it is switched on and no rule allows an action, the action is refused. This "deny by default" behaviour is what keeps data safe even though the publishable key is visible to every visitor of the website. Because the globe icons in Figure 9 suggest the tables are reachable through the API, checking RLS is an important part of this week.

| **Tables**                                            | **Visitors (not signed in)** | **Signed-in student** | **Signed-in administrator**      | **Reason**                                  |
|-------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| courses, modules, quizzes, mcqs, ai_summaries         | Read only                    | Read only             | Read and write their own content | Open-access study material (SRS FR-04).     |
| users, admins, students                               | No access                    | Own row only          | Own row only                     | Contain personal data and role information. |
| progress, progress_modules, enrollments, quiz_results | No access                    | Own rows only         | No access                        | Personal data of one student.               |

> **How to check**
>
> In the Supabase dashboard open **Authentication \> Policies**, or look at the table list: tables with RLS enabled are marked. Capture a screenshot that shows RLS enabled on all 12 tables. If any table shows it disabled, enable it and add the policies of the table above before the application is shown to anyone.

## 7. Authentication and Multi-Tenant Access

The brief asks for secure multi-tenant user authentication with signup, login, bcrypt password hashing and a session or JWT. This section first states what the screenshots show, then explains how each requirement is met by the technology the project uses, and finally lists what must still be proven.

### 7.1 What the Screenshots Show

| **Observation**                                                                              | **Figure** | **What it indicates**                                                                            |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| A login page exists at app/login/page.tsx and its file is open in the editor                 | 2, 6, 7    | A sign-in screen is part of the application.                                                     |
| The administrator page shows admin@ptut.com and a Logout button                              | 7          | A user session exists and a sign-out action is provided.                                         |
| The project contains the tables users, admins and students                                   | 9          | Accounts, roles and profiles are modelled in the database.                                       |
| The app folder contains only pages (no api folder); lib/supabase.ts is the only library file | 6          | Authentication is performed through the Supabase client, not through hand-written server routes. |
| The first commit is named "Week 5 scaffolding and auth setup"                                | 2, 4       | Authentication setup was part of the first delivery.                                             |

> **Not visible in the screenshots**
>
> The content of login/page.tsx, a signup form, a stored password value and a session token are not shown. This report therefore explains the mechanism and lists the proof to capture (Sections 7.7 and 8). Statements below that depend on the code are phrased as "indicated" and should be confirmed.

### 7.2 Approach: Supabase Auth

Supabase includes a managed authentication service (Supabase Auth). The application calls it through the same client that connects to the database. It satisfies each part of the brief:

| **Brief requirement**   | **How it is met**                                                                                                                                                                                              | **Where to see the proof**                                                         |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Signup                  | The sign-up action of the client creates an account from an e-mail and a password. The account is stored by Supabase in its own protected authentication area, separate from the tables the application reads. | Dashboard Authentication \> Users                                                  |
| bcrypt password hashing | Supabase Auth never stores the password itself. It stores a bcrypt hash with a random salt. The hash is not readable from the application's tables.                                                            | The password column is not visible anywhere in the Table Editor or the Users list. |
| Login                   | The sign-in action checks the password against the stored hash and, if it matches, creates a session. A wrong password gets a generic "invalid login credentials" answer.                                      | Behaviour of /login                                                                |
| Session / JWT           | A successful login returns an access token (a signed JWT, short-lived) and a refresh token. The client keeps them and renews the access token automatically.                                                   | Browser DevTools, Application tab: stored session                                  |
| Logout                  | The sign-out action ends the session and removes the tokens from the browser.                                                                                                                                  | Logout button in Figure 7                                                          |
| Multi-tenant isolation  | The JWT contains the user's id. Row Level Security rules in the database compare that id with the owner of each row, so a user can only reach their own data.                                                  | Dashboard Authentication \> Policies (Section 6.6)                                 |

> **If a custom login was written instead**
>
> If the login page uses its own hashing and tokens instead of Supabase Auth, the principles in the rest of this section still apply unchanged (bcrypt, signed tokens, role checks, isolation rules). Only the proof changes: instead of the Users list, show the stored hash in the database and the cookie or token in the browser.

### 7.3 Authentication Flows

Signup

1.  The visitor opens /login and chooses to create an account, then enters name, e-mail and password.

2.  The application sends the details to the authentication service over HTTPS.

3.  The service checks the format and the password length, and refuses an e-mail that already exists.

4.  The service hashes the password with bcrypt and stores the account. If e-mail confirmation is enabled, a confirmation message is sent and the first login waits for the click.

5.  The application creates the matching profile row (users and students) with the role STUDENT. The role is set by the application, never taken from the form.

Login

1.  The user enters e-mail and password on /login.

2.  The service compares the password with the stored hash. For any failure it returns the same generic message, so an attacker cannot tell whether the e-mail exists.

3.  On success the service returns the access token (JWT) and the refresh token, and the client stores them.

4.  The application reads the user's role and sends an administrator to /admin and a student to the home page.

Opening a protected page

1.  A request to /admin is made.

2.  The application checks for a valid session. Without one, the visitor is sent to /login.

3.  With a session, the application checks the role. A student is refused; an administrator is shown the page (Figure 7).

4.  Whatever the page shows, the database applies Row Level Security again, using the token's user id. This second check protects the data even if someone bypasses the page.

Logout

1.  The user presses **Logout** (Figure 7).

2.  The client ends the session and removes the tokens.

3.  The next request to /admin is redirected to /login.

### 7.4 Roles and Multi-Tenant Isolation

In CampusNotes a **tenant** is an owner of private data: each student owns their own progress and quiz history, and each administrator owns the courses they created. Multi-tenant security means one owner can never read or change another owner's data, even by guessing an identifier.

| **Actor**            | **Owns**                                                           | **May read**                              | **May write**    |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|------------------|
| Visitor (no account) | Nothing                                                            | Study catalog (courses, modules, quizzes) | Nothing          |
| Student              | Own progress, completed modules, enrollments, quiz results         | Catalog and own data                      | Own data only    |
| Administrator        | Courses they created, and the modules, quizzes and MCQs under them | Catalog and own content                   | Own content only |

Five rules keep the tenants apart:

1.  **Identity comes from the token, not from the form.** The user id used to decide ownership is the one inside the signed session, never a value typed or sent by the browser.

2.  **Every private table has an ownership rule** in Row Level Security that compares the row's owner with the token's user id.

3.  **The role is never chosen by the visitor.** The sign-up form must not contain a role field; administrator accounts are created by the project owner (for example in the dashboard), which is presumably how admin@ptut.com in Figure 7 was made.

4.  **Another owner's data looks missing,** so its existence is not revealed.

5.  **The secret key never reaches the browser.** Only the publishable key does (Figure 8).

> **Linking accounts and profiles**
>
> The authentication service keeps accounts in its own area, while the application keeps profile and role in users, admins and students. The two must share the same user id. Confirm that the id in users equals the id shown in **Authentication \> Users**, and that admin@ptut.com has role = ADMIN and a matching row in admins.

### 7.5 Why These Mechanisms Are Secure

bcrypt password hashing

| **Property**      | **Explanation**                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| One-way           | A hash cannot be turned back into the password. Even the project owner cannot read passwords.                                                                            |
| Salted            | A random value is added to each password before hashing, so two users with the same password get different hashes and pre-computed tables are useless.                   |
| Deliberately slow | bcrypt has a cost setting; each step doubles the work. Checking one password takes a fraction of a second, but guessing millions becomes very expensive for an attacker. |
| Self-describing   | The stored 60-character value contains the algorithm, the cost and the salt, so verification needs nothing else.                                                         |
| Length limit      | bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of a password, which is why very long passwords add nothing.                                                                         |

Session and JWT

A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a signed statement such as "this is user X, role authenticated, valid until time T". The service signs it with a secret, so nobody can change the statement without the signature failing. Because the token carries the user id, the database can apply the ownership rules without asking the application.

| **Part of the session** | **Purpose**                                                      | **Security point**                                              |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Access token (JWT)      | Sent with every request to prove who the user is                 | Short-lived, so a stolen copy stops working soon.               |
| Refresh token           | Obtains a new access token without asking for the password again | Longer-lived and stored by the client; it is rotated when used. |
| sub claim               | The user id                                                      | Used by Row Level Security as the owner id.                     |
| exp claim               | Expiry time                                                      | After this time the token is invalid.                           |

| **Setting**             | **Recommended value**                            | **Reason**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Minimum password length | 8 characters or more                             | The default in a new project is lower; length is the strongest protection.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Administrator session   | 30 minutes of inactivity (SRS NFR-08)            | Administrator accounts change all content. Check the session settings under Authentication in the dashboard; some session-length controls may depend on the plan, in which case the application can sign out an idle administrator itself. |
| E-mail confirmation     | On for the real system; may be off while testing | Proves the e-mail belongs to the user. The built-in e-mail sender has low sending limits, which is fine for testing.                                                                                                                       |
| Rate limiting           | Keep the service's defaults on                   | Slows password guessing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

### 7.6 Threats and Controls

| **Threat**                  | **Example**                                                  | **Control**                                                                                           |
|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Password guessing           | An attacker tries many passwords on one account              | bcrypt cost, minimum length, the service's rate limits, generic login error.                          |
| Finding which e-mails exist | Different messages for "unknown e-mail" and "wrong password" | One generic message for every login failure.                                                          |
| Stolen password database    | A leak of the stored hashes                                  | bcrypt with unique salts; hashes are not in the application's tables.                                 |
| Token theft                 | A script steals the session token                            | Short token lifetime; React escapes output; keep dependencies updated; never put secrets in the page. |
| Becoming an administrator   | Choosing ADMIN in a sign-up request                          | No role field in signup; the role is set on the server; admins are created by the owner.              |
| Reading another user's data | Changing an id in the address                                | Row Level Security compares the row owner with the token's user id.                                   |
| Direct database access      | Using the publishable key outside the website                | Row Level Security is on for every table; private tables have no public policy.                       |
| Secrets in the repository   | A key pushed to GitHub                                       | .env is ignored (Figure 4); only the publishable key is used in the browser.                          |
| Injection                   | SQL typed into a form                                        | The Supabase client sends parameterized requests; inputs are validated.                               |

## 10. Risks, Limitations and Next Steps

### 10.1 Risks

| **Risk**                                    | **Impact**                                     | **Mitigation**                                                                                |
|---------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| A key is committed or shown in a screenshot | Unauthorized access to the database            | .env stays ignored; only the publishable key in the browser; replace any exposed key at once. |
| Row Level Security left off on a table      | Anyone with the publishable key can read it    | Check the Policies page before every demonstration.                                           |
| Signup allows choosing a role               | Visitors become administrators                 | No role field in the form; roles set by the server or the owner.                              |
| Free-tier database paused after inactivity  | The demonstration fails                        | Open the dashboard and resume the project before presentations.                               |
| Direct commits to main                      | Broken code in the version the supervisor sees | Branch protection and the dev workflow (Sections 4.5 and 4.6).                                |

### 10.2 Known Limitations

- Only the Courses tab of the administrator page is visible; Modules and MCQ Banks are still to be built.

- Password reset by e-mail and social login are not part of Week 5.

- Session lifetimes depend on the settings available on the free plan.

- No automatic build check runs on pull requests yet.

### 10.3 Plan for Week 6

| **Task**                                                                          | **Result**                                         |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Make "+ Create Course" in Figure 7 save to the courses table and list the courses | Administrators can create and see courses.         |
| Edit and delete courses; restrict them to the owner                               | Ownership rule of Section 7.4 proven on real data. |
| Modules and MCQ Banks tabs                                                        | Content management complete (UC-11, UC-12).        |
| Home page and reader load courses and modules from the database                   | The public catalog works.                          |
| Save student progress and quiz results                                            | Student isolation proven (TC-14).                  |
| Add an automatic build check to pull requests                                     | The branch protection can require a green check.   |

## Appendix A: Glossary

| **Term**                     | **Meaning**                                                                                      |
|------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Scaffolding                  | The empty but correctly organized project structure created before features are written.         |
| Repository                   | A project folder whose full history is tracked by Git.                                           |
| Commit                       | A saved snapshot of the project with a message and an identifier.                                |
| Branch                       | A separate line of work. main is the main one.                                                   |
| Branch protection            | GitHub rules that stop direct pushes to a branch and require reviews or checks.                  |
| Pull request                 | A request to merge one branch into another, with review and checks.                              |
| App Router                   | The Next.js way of making pages from folders: a folder is an address, page.tsx is the screen.    |
| Environment variable         | A setting kept outside the code, for example the database address.                               |
| Publishable key / secret key | Supabase keys for browser code (limited by security rules) and for server code (full access).    |
| Row Level Security (RLS)     | Database rules that decide which rows each user may read or write.                               |
| bcrypt                       | A deliberately slow password-hashing function with a built-in random salt.                       |
| Salt                         | Random data added to each password before hashing.                                               |
| JWT                          | JSON Web Token: a signed statement (who, role, expiry) that cannot be changed without detection. |
| Session                      | The period during which a signed-in user is recognized.                                          |
| Multi-tenant                 | One system serving many owners whose data must stay separate.                                    |
